Kate was seventeen, and it was the first week of the summer holidays. Her friends were going to the beach, to the mountains or to their grandparents' houses. Kate wanted to go to Italy in August, but she didn't have enough money.

"You need a job," said her dad at breakfast.

"I know," said Kate. "But who wants a seventeen-year-old with no experience?"

That afternoon, she was walking past an old bookshop on Bridge Street when she saw a piece of paper in the window. It said: SUMMER HELP WANTED. MUST LIKE BOOKS AND CATS. ASK INSIDE.

Kate liked books very much. She wasn't sure about cats, but she opened the door anyway. A bell rang above her head.

The shop was dark and quiet, and it smelled of old paper. There were books everywhere: on the shelves, on the floor, on the chairs and even on the stairs. A large grey cat was sleeping on the counter.

"Hello?" Kate called.

An old man appeared from behind a tall pile of books. He had white hair, round glasses and a green cardigan.

"Yes?" he said.

"I saw your advertisement," said Kate. "I'd like the job."

The man looked at her over his glasses. Then he looked at the cat. "What do you think, Winston?" he asked.

The cat opened one yellow eye, looked at Kate, and closed it again.

"Good," said the old man. "He likes you. You can start tomorrow at nine."

The old man's name was Mr. Abbott. He had owned the shop for forty-five years. On Kate's first morning, he gave her a cup of tea and explained the rules.

"Rule number one," he said. "Never wake Winston. Rule number two: every customer must leave with the right book, not just any book. Rule number three: if you don't know where something is, ask the shop."

"Ask the shop?" said Kate.

Mr. Abbott smiled but didn't explain.

The first few days were hard. There was no computer and no list of books. Kate didn't know where anything was. A woman asked for a book about birds, and Kate looked for twenty minutes before she found it under a box of maps. A boy wanted a book about dinosaurs, but they only had one, and it was in French.

But slowly, Kate started to understand the shop. The books were not in alphabetical order. They were in a different kind of order. Books about the sea were near books about travel. Books about cooking were near books about gardens. Sad love stories were on the top shelf, "so you have to work a little to reach them," said Mr. Abbott.

By the end of the first week, when a customer asked for something, Kate often walked straight to the right shelf without thinking. It was a strange feeling, as if the shop was guiding her.

"You see?" said Mr. Abbott. "You asked the shop."

One rainy Tuesday, a woman came in with a boy of about twelve. The boy had his hands in his pockets and a very bored face.

"My son needs something to read for the summer," said the woman. "His teacher says so. But he hates reading."

"I don't hate it," said the boy. "It's just boring. Every book is boring."

Mr. Abbott was in the back room, so Kate had to help them. She remembered rule number two. Not just any book. The right book.

"What do you like doing?" she asked the boy.

He shrugged. "Football. Video games. Fixing my bike."

"What's the best thing that ever happened to you?"

The boy thought about it. "Last year my bike broke in the middle of a forest, and I fixed it with a stick and some string, and I rode home in the dark."

Kate smiled. She walked to a small shelf near the window, between books about mountains and books about machines. She took down a thin book with a picture of a boy and a broken bicycle on the cover. It was a story about a boy who rides across a whole country alone.

"Try the first page," she said. "If it's boring, you can give it back."

The boy read the first page. Then the second. Then he sat down on the floor and kept reading.

His mother looked at Kate with wide eyes. "How did you do that?"

Kate didn't know how to explain. "I asked the shop," she said.

At the end of July, Kate counted her money. She had enough for the trip to Italy. But she wasn't sure she wanted to go any more.

"Of course you must go," said Mr. Abbott, when she told him. "Travel is like reading. You come back a different person."

"But who will help you in the shop?"

Mr. Abbott was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "I'm going to tell you a secret. I'm eighty-one years old, Kate. I'm tired. I've been thinking of closing the shop for a long time. That's why I put the paper in the window. I wanted to see if someone could still hear it."

"Hear what?"

"The shop," he said simply. "Most people can't. You can."

Kate went to Italy. She saw old cities, blue seas and narrow streets full of flowers. In every town, she found a small bookshop and went inside. She always bought one book, and she always thought of Mr. Abbott and Winston.

When she came back, there was a new sign in the window on Bridge Street. It said: ABBOTT AND WEST, BOOKSELLERS. Kate's family name was West.

Mr. Abbott was behind the counter, drinking tea. Winston was asleep next to him.

"I thought you could work on Saturdays while you finish school," said Mr. Abbott. "And after that, we'll see."

Kate looked around the dark, quiet shop full of books. It felt like coming home.

"Rule number one," she said. "Never wake Winston."

When their grandfather died, Ben and his younger sister Mia were sent to help their parents clear out his house by the sea. It was a tall, narrow building at the end of a long road, with a garden full of wild roses and a roof that leaked whenever it rained.

Neither of them had spent much time there. Grandad had been a quiet, private man who had worked all his life as a ship's engineer. He sent birthday cards with five-pound notes inside, and once, when Ben was eight, he had shown him how to tie a sailor's knot. That was almost all they knew about him.

"You two can start with the attic," said their mother on the first morning. "Put anything that looks important in a box, and anything that looks like rubbish in a bag. If you're not sure, ask me."

The attic was hot and dusty and full of things that nobody had touched for decades: broken chairs, old suitcases, piles of yellow newspapers and a rocking horse with one ear missing. A small round window let in a narrow beam of sunlight.

"This is going to take forever," complained Mia, who was thirteen and had wanted to spend the summer with her friends.

Ben didn't answer. He had found a wooden chest under the window, half hidden by a blanket. It was locked, but the lock was so old that it broke when he pulled it.

Inside, wrapped in a piece of oilcloth, was a folded sheet of thick paper. When he opened it carefully, he saw that it was a hand-drawn map.

The map showed a stretch of coastline that both of them recognised at once. There was the little harbour, the church with the crooked tower, and the long beach where they had played as small children. But there were other things too: tiny symbols they didn't understand, a dotted line that wound along the cliffs, and, at the end of it, a small black cross.

At the bottom, in their grandfather's neat handwriting, were the words: For whoever finds this first. Follow the line at low tide.

"It's a treasure map," said Mia, suddenly interested. "An actual treasure map."

"Don't be silly," said Ben, although his heart was beating faster. "Grandad was an engineer, not a pirate."

They showed it to their mother at lunch. She looked at it for a long time and then laughed softly.

"He used to do this when I was a girl," she said. "He made maps for me and my brother and hid little presents along the beach. A shell, a coin, a chocolate bar. I'd forgotten all about it."

"So it's just a game?" asked Mia, disappointed.

"Probably. But this one looks newer than the ones he made for us. Look at the paper." She turned it over. In the corner, written in pencil, was a date from only two years ago.

Ben checked the tide tables on his phone. Low tide was at six o'clock the next morning.

"We're going," he said.

They left the house before anyone else was awake. The air was cold and grey, and a thin mist lay over the sea. The tide had gone out a long way, leaving wet sand, rock pools and long ribbons of seaweed.

Following the dotted line was harder than they had expected. The map didn't show distances, and some of the symbols turned out to be rocks that only appeared at low tide. One of them looked exactly like a sleeping dog, which made Mia laugh out loud. Another was a narrow gap between two cliffs that they would never have noticed if they hadn't been looking for it.

"How long have we got?" asked Mia, as they squeezed through the gap.

Ben looked at his watch. "About an hour before the water starts coming back. After that, we can't get out this way."

Behind the cliffs was a tiny hidden beach, completely invisible from the path above. At the back of it, in the rock, was the entrance to a shallow cave. Someone had painted a small white cross above it, now almost washed away by the weather.

Inside the cave it was dry and surprisingly warm. On a ledge at the back, wrapped in the same kind of oilcloth as the map, was a metal box about the size of a shoebox.

They looked at each other. Neither of them wanted to be the one to open it.

"Together," said Mia, and they lifted the lid.

There was no gold inside the box. There were no jewels or coins. Instead, there was a thick notebook with a leather cover, a small brass compass, and an envelope with their names on it: Ben and Mia.

Ben opened the envelope with shaking fingers and read the letter aloud.

"Dear Ben and Mia, if you are reading this, then you found the map, and you were curious enough and brave enough to follow it. I am sorry I was not a better grandfather. I was never good at talking, but I have always been good at making things. This notebook is the story of my life at sea: the places I saw, the storms I survived, and the people I loved. I wrote it for you, because I didn't know how to say these things out loud. The compass belonged to my own father. It has never been wrong. I hope it helps you find your way. With love, Grandad."

For a while, neither of them spoke. Outside, they could hear the sea slowly coming back.

"We need to go," said Ben at last, putting the notebook carefully inside his jacket.

They ran back along the beach as the first waves began to cover the sand. When they reached the path, they were wet to the knees and out of breath, but they were both laughing.

That evening, the whole family sat in Grandad's kitchen while Mia read the first chapter of the notebook aloud. It began on a cold morning in 1962, when a nervous seventeen-year-old boy stepped onto a ship for the very first time.

By the time she stopped reading, it was after midnight. Nobody wanted her to stop.
